prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping

statement.case_for: I keep B030 as a single-part prize and my position has not changed since round 1. After the full exchange, the case rests on three points that I can check against the record. First, the invention is original and separable from earlier prizes: Katori's 2001-2003 proposal that trapping at the magic wavelength cancels the light shift is a different idea from the 2005 frequency comb and the 2012 control of single ions. Second, it is verified in the way I trust most. Independent laboratories in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and China have reproduced it and compare clocks at about 1e-18. Third, the credit is the most defensible of any shortlisted candidate: Katori for the proposal and first demonstration, Ye for taking the accuracy and the many-body regime to the present level. I propose a citation that names the lattice clock and its magic-wavelength realization and says nothing about applications. That answers the chair's first question and keeps the wording from overlapping with 2005 and 2012.
statement.case_against: My reservations are narrower than before but not gone. A strict reading of 'discovery or invention' leaves a real question about whether a record in precision is more than a refinement of work already honoured, and I would want the committee to say that it accepts the lattice clock as an invention in the statutory sense and not merely as a very good instrument. The societal benefit is mostly prospective, because the SI second has not been redefined and the dark-matter and constants searches have produced bounds, not detections. Priority outside the two names is also not closed: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the Yb pioneers have claims that expert reviewers should document. If a reviewer shows that an early demonstration predates Katori's first experiment or that the magic-wavelength idea has a separate originator, I would reopen the two-name credit.

responses.point: Kroll accepts B030 as a measurement achievement that changed what can be measured, while naming the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and the early contributors outside the credited names as real objections.
responses.response: I agree that these objections are real and I also agree they are not decisive. On the question of the statutory sense, I would put the line where you put it, at the invention: the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a new instrument concept with a new physical principle, and it is verified. I do not want the citation to rest on geodesy, dark-matter searches or the redefinition of the second, because those are demonstrations and prospects. Your Hall-laboratory link to Ye is a mentor-lineage tie without collaboration, and I do not see that it requires recusal. I would still ask you to say whether you think it affects your reading of Ye's share.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B030 first on the atomic-physics argument that magic-wavelength trapping is a new idea resting on polarizability, and says the split between the proposal and the Boulder realization can be argued.
responses.response: You have not yet answered the share question I put to you in round 1, and it is the main thing I still need before I vote. Does the originality sit with Katori's proposal and early Sr demonstration, with Ye's accuracy and many-body work, or in equal parts? I take your point that you may be biased upward because you are close to the field, and I am therefore asking for the record of who did what first, not for your overall view. I also need you to separate the Lemonde and Takamoto claims into what was a proposal, what was a demonstration, and what was an accuracy result. If they are demonstrations that came after Katori's, the two names stand; if any came before, we should know now.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B020 (IceCube) to B030 and says he has not found a second part that is both distinct and fairly attributed within the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree that a second part does not work, and I have looked for one. B020 is the nearest in scientific quality, but three names from a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND behind them and the source picture still forming, is something I cannot say I am absolutely sure of. B058 and B017 each omit people with strong claims. A second part would also take us to four or five names or leave the credit contestable, and it would add nothing to B030. I therefore support a single-part prize and keep B020 as my first alternative. If expert reviewers document the three IceCube names convincingly, I would reconsider it for another year.

responses.point: Danielsson keeps B055 (Bennett, Spergel, Puget) first as the measurement of the age, geometry and composition of the universe, says no earlier prize covers this era, but concedes that only he and the chair ranked it, calls the WMAP-Planck and Page-Puget allocation a real problem, and says he would not be unhappy to see B030 win.
responses.response: I take your point that the 2019 prize was theoretical and left the measurement side open, and I accept that percent-level parameters go beyond what COBE established. My difficulty is that I read the original discovery of the anisotropies as the COBE experiment, and I apply the same test to every candidate: original experiment, not a later and better one. That makes precision mapping a refinement for me, even though a very important one. The credit problem you describe is independent of that and by itself prevents me from ranking it first. I would reconsider if you can give a clear account of what among Bennett, Spergel, Puget and Page was a discovery that COBE had not made.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B049 (Kardar and Zhang) as a simple mechanism with exact one-dimensional results and liquid-crystal experiments, while he accepts that it is a minority view and that Parisi is outside the credited names.
responses.response: I appreciate that you said openly that you are in the minority. My concern is the one you raise yourself. The experimental verification is narrow, essentially the liquid-crystal turbulence work, and the 1986 paper had a third author who already shares the 2021 prize. The prize is for something verified by experiment, so the weak experimental side matters more to me than the elegance of the theory. I also note that Zhang has died, and the historical record of who did the original work would call for naming him. I would like to know whether your concern about the B030 attribution is scientific or only a matter of preferring a theory prize.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B058 to B030 but says the physics of a new class of quantum matter is arguably deeper than an instrument and that he would not object to B058 as an outcome.
responses.response: I understand that view and I do not dismiss the depth of topological insulators. For me the issue remains credit and verification. Quantized edge conduction in HgTe is imperfect, as you note, and any three-name set omits Bernevig, Hughes and Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan, which cannot be reconciled with my wish to be sure that the people credited did the original work. I would be willing to look at B058 again if the experts give a clear account of who predicted and who observed what. At present that is more uncertain than the B030 attribution.

uncertainties: Whether expert reviewers find a priority claim by Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or others strong enough to change the two-name credit, and how the share between Katori and Ye should be described.
Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement invention as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether the citation can be worded narrowly enough to avoid overlap with the frequency-comb and ion-control prizes without understating the invention.
How far the societal benefit is demonstrated rather than prospective, given that the redefinition of the second is still pending.
Whether B020 or B017 can be given a defensible three-name credit by expert review, which I would then weigh against B030 in the vote.
statement.conflict_note: I have been a Fellow of the University of Tokyo since 2025 and have had exchanges with that university for more than ten years, and Hidetoshi Katori is, to my knowledge, based there (and at RIKEN). I have no collaboration, joint publication, funding or personal tie to Katori or Jun Ye. I regard this as an institutional connection and not a personal conflict, and I would accept the committee's decision if it wants me to recuse myself or discount my vote on B030. I do not think Kroll's link to Ye's mentor lineage requires recusal. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is a committee member and not a candidate. I have no other conflict.
